stem: A 70 kg patient in septic shock (BP 85/50, HR 120) needs intubation. Which induction agent is most appropriate?
explanation:
Why ketamine: it preserves (actually augments) sympathetic tone — in shock it maintains MAP via endogenous catecholamine release. Dose-reduce to 0.5-1 mg/kg in catecholamine-depleted patients.

Why not the others: Propofol causes profound vasodilation + cardiodepression — arrest in borderline BP; Etomidate is haemodynamically neutral but transient adrenal suppression (1 dose) — still used but the sepsis-specific benefit of ketamine favours it; Midazolam alone is unreliable induction and still drops BP.

Pearl: "Push-dose" phenylephrine 50-200 μg or noradrenaline 10-20 μg at the bedside before/during intubation blunts post-induction hypotension. Give 500 mL crystalloid pre-RSI if time allows.

Pitfall: fentanyl 'co-induction' may crash the already-hypotensive patient — omit or halve.
ref: Jabre P et al. KETASED. Lancet 2009;374:293-300

stem: Which of the following is the single best bedside predictor of difficult bag-mask ventilation?
explanation:
Why beard + edentulous: both wreck the mask seal. The MOANS mnemonic for difficult BMV — Mask seal (beard, blood), Obese/obstruction, Age > 55, No teeth, Stiff lungs. Three or more = anticipate difficult ventilation.

Why not others: Mallampati and male sex predict difficult laryngoscopy, not BMV; thick neck (> 43 cm in males) suggests difficult intubation + OSA but is less predictive of BMV than mask-seal issues.

Pearl: for the edentulous patient, leave dentures IN for BMV and remove them only for laryngoscopy. Two-person BMV with jaw-thrust almost always rescues a failing one-person seal.

Pitfall: "I'll just intubate" without confirming you can BMV — if you can't ventilate and can't intubate, you're in CICO and need the surgical airway drill immediately.
ref: Langeron O et al. Prediction of difficult mask ventilation. Anesthesiology 2000;92:1229-36

stem: A 90 kg patient needs RSI. You chose rocuronium. What is the optimal dose and reversal plan?
explanation:
Why 1.2 mg/kg + sugammadex: RSI dose of rocuronium is 1.0-1.2 mg/kg — matches succinylcholine's onset (~ 45-60 s) but lasts 45-70 min. Sugammadex 16 mg/kg encapsulates rocuronium directly and reverses even profound block within 3 minutes — this is the modern 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' rescue.

Why not others: 0.6 mg/kg is the intubating (not RSI) dose — slower onset ~ 90 s; neostigmine needs some spontaneous recovery (TOF > 1) — it cannot reverse deep block; 1.5 mg/kg is excessive; 'no reversal' is historically correct but outdated since sugammadex.

Pearl: for maintenance reversal (post-op) use sugammadex 2-4 mg/kg based on TOF.

Pitfall: sugammadex binds hormonal contraceptives — advise backup contraception for 7 days.
ref: Jahr JS et al. Sugammadex vs neostigmine. Anesth Analg 2015;121:1573-83

stem: During intubation attempt for severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.10, PaCO₂ 20), bag-mask ventilation is briefly interrupted. Minutes later the patient arrests. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Loss of respiratory compensation → acute acidaemia and cardiovascular collapse
explanation:
Why 'loss of respiratory compensation': in severe HAGMA the patient is driving PaCO₂ to ~ 20 to maintain pH 7.10. Any apnoea → CO₂ jumps 5 mmHg per minute → pH tumbles → myocardial depression, vasoplegia, arrest. This is the peri-intubation acidaemic arrest — one of the deadliest moments in ICU.

Why not others: hypoxaemia is important but SpO₂ drop is usually gradual and reversible; vagal response causes bradycardia not acute arrest; sux-induced K⁺ rise is < 0.5 mEq/L in a normal patient.

Pearl: for severe acidosis match the patient's minute ventilation on the ventilator the moment they are paralysed. Pre-empt with bicarbonate (if pH < 7.10) and consider awake intubation (ketamine + topical) to avoid apnoea.

Pitfall: standard vent settings (RR 12, TV 500) → iatrogenic arrest in minutes.
ref: Weingart SD, Levitan RM. Preoxygenation and prevention of desaturation during emergency airway management. Ann Emerg Med 2012;59:165-75

stem: Correct positioning for direct laryngoscopy in an obese patient is:
explanation:
Why ramped: pillows/towels/commercial ramp under shoulders, neck and head so the external auditory meatus lies in the same horizontal plane as the sternal notch. This aligns oral-pharyngeal-laryngeal axes AND improves FRC (lower diaphragm) giving more apnoeic oxygenation time.

Why not others: flat supine in obesity closes airways within seconds; Trendelenburg collapses them further and worsens reflux; reverse Trendelenburg helps FRC but does not align the axes.

Pearl: 25-30° head-up PLUS ramp — best of both. Apnoeic oxygenation (nasal cannula 15 L/min left on through intubation) buys another 2-3 minutes.

Pitfall: ramping makes the view easier but moves the laryngoscope hand position — rehearse with the ramped patient before giving paralytic.
ref: Collins JS et al. Laryngoscopy and morbid obesity. Obes Surg 2004;14:1171-5

stem: Which drug combination gives the fastest intubating conditions?
explanation:
Why succinylcholine: onset 30-45 s, peak block at 60 s — fastest paralytic available. Etomidate reaches peak hypnotic effect within 30 s. Combined, ideal intubating conditions in ~ 60 s.

Why not others: rocuronium 0.6 mg/kg onset ~ 90-120 s (use 1.2 mg/kg to match sux); vecuronium even slower (2-3 min); midazolam induction is unreliable.

Pearl: succinylcholine contraindications — hyperkalaemia, burns > 48 h old, prolonged immobility, denervation injury, malignant hyperthermia history, severe muscular dystrophy. In any of these → use rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg.

Pitfall: succinylcholine fasciculations can raise K⁺ by 0.5 mEq/L — dangerous in borderline hyperkalaemia.
ref: Mallon WK et al. Rocuronium vs succinylcholine for RSI. J Emerg Med 2009;37:183-8

stem: Three intubation attempts fail, BMV is becoming difficult, SpO₂ 82 %. Next step?
options: Call for help and prepare front-of-neck access
Give more sedation and try nasal intubation
Give reversal, let patient wake up
explanation:
Why FONA: this is CICO (can't intubate, can't oxygenate). After 3 failed attempts + failing BMV + desaturation, declare failure and move to front-of-neck access (scalpel-bougie-tube or needle cricothyroidotomy). The algorithm (DAS 2015) is declared, timed and spoken out loud.

Why not others: a 4th attempt wastes time with falling SpO₂; nasal intubation requires skills and time you don't have; letting the patient wake assumes drugs will wear off — sux might, but roc won't (unless sugammadex ready), and the patient is already apnoeic.

Pearl: sugammadex 16 mg/kg IF rocuronium was given — may restore spontaneous breathing within 3 min. Does NOT help if succinylcholine was used or if BMV alone is inadequate.

Pitfall: "one more try" is the commonest cause of CICO deaths — commit to the surgical airway early.
ref: Frerk C et al. Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines. Br J Anaesth 2015;115:827-48

stem: A 65-year-old asthmatic in status asthmaticus needs intubation. Best induction agent?
explanation:
Why ketamine: direct bronchodilator (catecholamine release + direct smooth-muscle effect). Preserves haemodynamics. Dose 1-2 mg/kg IV. Can also use as infusion 0.5-1 mg/kg/hr for severe bronchospasm.

Why not others: propofol is neutral to bronchodilation but drops BP (bad in already-hyperinflated patient with high intrathoracic pressure); etomidate is neutral on airway; thiopentone can trigger bronchospasm.

Pearl: after intubating an asthmatic, set vent to allow prolonged expiration — RR 8-10, I:E 1:4-1:5, TV 6 mL/kg, permissive hypercapnia pH ≥ 7.20. Watch for dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP).

Pitfall: rapid respiratory rate on vent worsens breath-stacking → tension physiology → PEA arrest. Disconnect and manually decompress if BP crashes.
ref: Reynolds SF, Heffner J. Airway management of the critically ill patient. Chest 2005;127:1397-412

stem: pH 7.22 · PaCO₂ 20 · HCO₃ 8 · Na 140 · Cl 100 · albumin 4. What is the primary disorder and is compensation appropriate?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
explanation:
Why 'appropriate compensation': HAGMA (AG = 140 − 100 − 8 = 32). Winters' expected PaCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃) + 8 ± 2 = 20 ± 2. Measured = 20 → exactly within compensation range → pure HAGMA with appropriate (not additional) respiratory response.

Why not others: 'under-compensated' is wrong (PaCO₂ is at the expected value); 'mixed with respiratory alkalosis' would require PaCO₂ < 18 (over-breathing beyond compensation); 'primary respiratory alkalosis' would show pH > 7.45.

Pearl: ALWAYS calculate Δ-Δ in HAGMA: ΔAG = 32 − 12 = 20; ΔHCO₃ = 24 − 8 = 16. Ratio 1.25 (0.8-2.0 = pure HAGMA). < 0.8 → added NAGMA (e.g. diarrhoea); > 2.0 → added met alkalosis (e.g. vomiting).

Pitfall: correct AG for albumin: AG_corr = AG + 2.5 × (4 − albumin). Hypoalbuminaemia hides a true HAGMA.
ref: Winters RW. Ann NY Acad Sci 1966;133:211-24

stem: Causes of a HIGH anion gap metabolic acidosis include all EXCEPT:
explanation:
Why diarrhoea is NAGMA: loss of HCO₃-rich fluid is replaced by Cl from saline → hyperchloraemic (normal AG) acidosis. HAGMA requires an unmeasured anion — ketones, lactate, toxic alcohols, uraemic acids.

Why the rest ARE HAGMA: methanol → formate; DKA → β-hydroxybutyrate; salicylate → salicylate itself + lactate.

Pearl: MUDPILES mnemonic for HAGMA — Methanol, Uraemia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Isoniazid / Iron, Lactate, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates. For NAGMA use HARDUP — Hyperalimentation / hyperchloraemia, Acetazolamide / Addison's, RTA, Diarrhoea, Ureteroileostomy, Pancreatic/biliary fistula.

Pitfall: normal saline resuscitation can CAUSE a NAGMA — switch to balanced solution (Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte) in large-volume resus.
ref: Kraut JA, Madias NE. Treatment of acute metabolic acidosis. Nat Rev Nephrol 2012

stem: An intubated patient on FiO₂ 60 % and PEEP 10 has PaO₂ 75. What is the P/F ratio and ARDS severity (Berlin)?
explanation:
Why 125 / moderate: P/F = PaO₂ ÷ FiO₂ (expressed as decimal) = 75 ÷ 0.6 = 125. Berlin (2012): mild 200-300 · moderate 100-200 · severe < 100, all on PEEP ≥ 5.

Why not others: severe would need P/F < 100; 450 would assume FiO₂ in percent (wrong — always divide by decimal); 1.25 confuses FiO₂ units.

Pearl: SpO₂/FiO₂ (S/F) ratio tracks P/F when ABG not available: S/F 315 ≈ P/F 300, S/F 235 ≈ P/F 200. Useful at bedside without a line.

Pitfall: a patient breathing 2 L nasal cannula (~ FiO₂ 28 %) with PaO₂ 80 has P/F 285 — still Berlin mild ARDS if the clinical picture fits. Don't dismiss hypoxaemia just because they're not on high FiO₂.
ref: ARDS Definition Task Force. Berlin definition. JAMA 2012;307:2526-33

stem: A 55-year-old presents after methanol ingestion. ABG: pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 22, HCO₃ 10. Na 142, Cl 100, measured osm 320, calculated osm 290. The best initial antidote is:
explanation:
Why fomepizole: potent competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase — blocks conversion of methanol → formate (the toxic metabolite). Dose 15 mg/kg load → 10 mg/kg q 12 h × 4 → 15 mg/kg q 12 h until methanol < 20 mg/dL. Add folate 50 mg IV q 6 h to accelerate formate clearance.

Why not others: ethanol works via same mechanism but causes CNS depression, needs levels q 1-2 h, and competes with CNS drugs; pyridoxine is for isoniazid toxicity + ethylene glycol adjunct; methylene blue is for methaemoglobinaemia.

Pearl: HD indication in methanol: pH < 7.15, methanol level > 50 mg/dL, visual symptoms, renal failure. Osmolal gap > 10 + HAGMA + consistent history = toxic alcohol until proven otherwise.

Pitfall: normal osmolal gap does NOT exclude methanol — late presenters have already metabolised it to formate (which raises AG but not osm gap).
ref: Kraut JA, Mullins ME. Toxic alcohols. NEJM 2018;378:270-80

stem: pH 7.52 · PaCO₂ 48 · HCO₃ 38 · K 2.8 · Cl 90. Best interpretation?
options: Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
explanation:
Why metabolic alkalosis + compensation: pH alkalaemic, HCO₃ ↑ (primary) with ↑ PaCO₂ (hypoventilation compensation). Expected PaCO₂ = 0.7 × HCO₃ + 20 ± 5 = 0.7 × 38 + 20 = 47 ± 5 → measured 48 fits perfectly.

Why not others: respiratory alkalosis would have ↓ PaCO₂; mixed would need PaCO₂ < 42 (over-compensation).

Pearl: saline-responsive (urine Cl < 20): vomiting, diuretic use, NG suction → replace volume + K + Cl. Saline-resistant (urine Cl > 20): hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's, Bartter, exogenous steroid → treat the cause, spironolactone.

Pitfall: severe met alkalosis (pH > 7.55) impairs oxygen delivery (left-shifts oxyhaemoglobin curve) and causes seizures, arrhythmias. Acetazolamide 250-500 mg IV may help if volume overloaded.
ref: Galla JH. Metabolic alkalosis. JASN 2000;11:369-75

stem: An intubated COPD patient: PaO₂ 180 on FiO₂ 40 %. Calculate A-a gradient (age 60, PB 760 at sea level).
explanation:
Why ~ 0: A-a = PAO₂ − PaO₂. PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (760 − 47) − PaCO₂/0.8 ≈ 0.4 × 713 − 50 = 285 − 62 = 223. So gradient ≈ 223 − 180 = 43 — actually option 3 (~ 50). Let me recalc: normal 'expected' A-a = age/4 + 4 = 19 at this age. Measured 43 suggests V/Q mismatch (very typical of COPD).

Why not others: if truly healthy lungs the gradient would match expected (10-20); 100 would be dramatic shunt.

Pearl: normal A-a < age/4 + 4 on room air. ↑ A-a differential: V/Q mismatch (PE, pneumonia, COPD), diffusion defect (fibrosis), shunt (ARDS, cardiac). Normal A-a with hypoxia → hypoventilation or low FiO₂ or high altitude.

Pitfall: at supra-physiologic FiO₂ (> 50 %) gradient becomes less reliable — pure shunt fraction (Qs/Qt) is a better measure.
ref: Petersson J, Glenny RW. Gas exchange and ventilation-perfusion relationships. Eur Respir J 2014;44:1023-41

stem: When is IV sodium bicarbonate indicated in metabolic acidosis?
options: pH < 7.20 with ongoing severe acidaemia from TCA / salicylate / hyperkalaemia; or renal failure
explanation:
Why selective indications: bicarbonate's role in non-specific acidaemia is limited. Clear indications: TCA overdose (alkalinisation antagonises Na-channel blockade), severe salicylate OD (traps ionised salicylate out of CNS/urine), hyperkalaemia with acidosis as adjunct, severe acidaemia in AKI/uraemic acidosis (BICAR-ICU 2018).

Why not others: DKA responds to insulin + fluid; bicarb only if pH < 6.9 (ADA guidance); in lactic acidosis from sepsis bicarb neither improves haemodynamics nor mortality (SSC 2021 'may consider' at pH < 7.2 + AKI).

Pearl: bicarbonate deficit = 0.5 × weight × (24 − HCO₃). Give half slowly, recheck ABG and K⁺ (bicarb shifts K intracellularly).

Pitfall: bicarb → CO₂ + water. In an under-ventilated patient PaCO₂ rises (worsening intracellular acidosis), Ca drops (tetany), Na rises (hypernatraemia).
ref: Jaber S et al. BICAR-ICU. Lancet 2018;392:31-40

stem: Per the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021, how quickly should broad-spectrum antibiotics be given in septic shock?
explanation:
Why 1 hour: STRONG recommendation SSC 2021 for septic shock + probable sepsis. Every hour of delay > 1 h = 7.6 % relative mortality increase (Kumar 2006). Draw cultures only if it does NOT delay antibiotics.

Why not others: 3 hours is the window for 'possible' sepsis without shock (investigate first); 6 hours is too late in shock; cultures-first is historical and costs lives.

Pearl: SSC 2021 'hour-1 bundle' = lactate + cultures + broad-spectrum antibiotics + 30 mL/kg crystalloid + vasopressor if MAP < 65 after fluid.

Pitfall: "narrow" antibiotics without source cover (e.g. only gram-positive cover in urosepsis) — start BROAD, de-escalate after cultures. Source control (drain, debride, remove catheter) is as important as antibiotics.
ref: Evans L et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143

stem: A 70 kg patient in septic shock has lactate 6, MAP 55 on 1 L crystalloid. Next best step?
options: Start noradrenaline peripheral, titrate to MAP ≥ 65; continue crystalloid to 30 mL/kg total
explanation:
Why early noradrenaline + continuing fluid: SSC 2021 — 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid in first 3 h for hypoperfusion. But don't delay vasopressor if MAP < 65 after initial fluid; start noradrenaline through a large peripheral IV while placing central line. Combined approach restores MAP faster and prevents fluid overload (CENSER 2019).

Why not others: vasopressin is add-on AFTER noradrenaline (at ~ 0.25-0.5 μg/kg/min); hydrocortisone comes in at refractory shock (noradrenaline > 0.25); albumin bolus not first-line (ALBIOS showed no benefit).

Pearl: dynamic fluid responsiveness (PLR, PPV) better than CVP after initial resus.

Pitfall: chasing a MAP target with liters of saline → interstitial oedema, ARDS, ileus, delayed weaning.
ref: Evans L et al. SSC 2021 · Permpikul C. CENSER. AJRCCM 2019;199:1097-105

stem: The qSOFA criteria include all EXCEPT:
explanation:
Why lactate is excluded: qSOFA was designed as a bedside non-lab screen — RR, GCS, BP. Score ≥ 2 → look harder, probable sepsis with poor outcome.

Why the others are IN: RR ≥ 22, altered mentation (GCS < 15), SBP ≤ 100 — all available without a lab.

Pearl: qSOFA has LOW sensitivity for sepsis early (missed by 40 %) but HIGH specificity for mortality once positive. Use as a prompt to escalate, not to rule out.

Pitfall: waiting for qSOFA ≥ 2 before starting workup delays care. Use NEWS-2 or clinical gestalt for screening; qSOFA for risk-stratifying the already-recognised patient.
ref: Singer M et al. Sepsis-3. JAMA 2016;315:801-10

stem: A septic-shock patient remains on noradrenaline 0.35 μg/kg/min with MAP 62 after full resuscitation. What has the clearest evidence for mortality benefit at this point?
explanation:
Why hydrocortisone: APROCCHSS (NEJM 2018) showed 90-day mortality 43 vs 49 % (NNT ~ 17) with hydrocortisone 200 mg/day + fludrocortisone in septic shock on vasopressors > 0.25 μg/kg/min. ADRENAL (same year, larger n) showed faster shock reversal and shorter ventilation, no overall mortality benefit.

Why not others: vasopressin (VAAST 2008) reduces catecholamine load — no mortality benefit alone; angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) rescues extreme vasoplegia — no mortality benefit; vit C 'metabolic bundle' (VICTAS, LOVIT) failed to show benefit, LOVIT showed harm.

Pearl: add vasopressin and hydrocortisone concurrently once noradrenaline > 0.25 — catecholamine-sparing + mortality signal.

Pitfall: continuing just to escalate noradrenaline past 1 μg/kg/min without adjuncts → peripheral ischaemia, splanchnic hypoperfusion, arrhythmias.
ref: Annane D et al. APROCCHSS. NEJM 2018;378:809-18

stem: Which is the strongest indicator of adequate resuscitation in septic shock?
explanation:
Why lactate clearance: normalisation of lactate (to < 2) or clearance > 10 %/hr correlates with tissue perfusion and reduced mortality (LACTATES trial, ANDROMEDA-SHOCK secondary). Capillary refill time (CRT < 3 s) is a non-inferior bedside alternative (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK primary).

Why not others: CVP target 8-12 has been abandoned (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe); MAP > 65 is a floor, not an endpoint; UO is laggy and affected by diuretics.

Pearl: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (JAMA 2019) → CRT-guided resuscitation non-inferior to lactate-guided; less fluid, less organ failure.

Pitfall: persistent lactate ≠ ongoing shock — think of liver clearance, β-agonist (adrenaline), metformin, thiamine deficiency.
ref: Hernández G et al. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK. JAMA 2019;321:654-64

stem: Source control for intra-abdominal sepsis should ideally occur:
explanation:
Why within 12 h: SSC 2021 recommends 'as soon as medically and logistically practical', with observational data showing increased mortality beyond 12 h (and sharp rise beyond 24). For perforation, obstruction, infected necrosis, cholangitis — drainage / surgery is as crucial as antibiotics.

Why not others: 6 h is aspirational but often impractical; 24 h too late; 'after full resus' is a false choice — resuscitate AND intervene concurrently.

Pearl: source types — abscess (drain), necrotic tissue (debride), infected catheter (remove), obstruction (decompress), empyema (chest tube), septic arthritis (washout).

Pitfall: "the patient is too unstable for theatre" — often the UNDRAINED source IS why they're unstable. Discuss early with surgery, anaesthesia.
ref: Evans L et al. SSC 2021

stem: The most sensitive biomarker to monitor antibiotic de-escalation in bacterial sepsis is:
explanation:
Why procalcitonin (PCT): rises within 2-4 h of bacterial infection, falls with source control + effective antibiotics. PROACT trial and others show PCT-guided algorithms safely shorten antibiotic duration by 1-2 days.

Why not others: WBC is non-specific and slow; CRP peaks at 48 h and is not organism-specific; lactate reflects perfusion, not infection.

Pearl: PCT < 0.25 ng/mL in stable patient → consider stopping antibiotics (per PCT algorithms). PCT > 2 at 24-48 h with clinical worsening → source still uncontrolled.

Pitfall: PCT is NOT a 'is this sepsis?' test — it elevates in surgery, trauma, pancreatitis, burns. Use it serially for trend, not as a one-off diagnostic.
ref: de Jong E et al. ProACT. Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:819-27

stem: Which intervention has shown mortality benefit in severe ARDS (P/F < 150)?
explanation:
Why proning: PROSEVA (NEJM 2013) in moderate-severe ARDS (P/F < 150) → 28-day mortality 16 vs 32.8 % (NNT 6). ≥ 16 h/day, usually within 48 h of intubation, continues until P/F > 150 at supine for 4 h on FiO₂ ≤ 0.6 + PEEP ≤ 10.

Why not others: iNO improves oxygenation (bridge) — no mortality signal; HFOV HARMFUL in adults (OSCILLATE early-stopped); steroids (DEXA-ARDS) help moderate-severe ARDS but are a separate category (not THE mortality intervention).

Pearl: PROSEVA was done in centres with expertise — needs team drill (airway secured, lines accessible, eye protection, 4-6 staff for turn).

Pitfall: complications — ETT displacement, pressure ulcers, brachial plexus injury. Reposition arms q 2 h in the 'swimmer' position.
ref: Guérin C et al. PROSEVA. NEJM 2013;368:2159-68

stem: A 70 kg (PBW) ARDS patient needs tidal volume set. What is the target range?
explanation:
Why 4-8 mL/kg PBW (aim 6): ARDSnet 2000 — 6 mL/kg PBW reduced mortality 22 % vs 12 mL/kg. PBW scales with height, not fat — use the Devine formula (male: 50 + 2.3×(ht_inches − 60); female: 45.5 + 2.3×(ht_inches − 60)).

Why not others: actual weight overdoses obese patients (big belly, small lung); 8-10 mL/kg PBW is the old 'physiologic' recommendation that killed people; SpO₂-only ignores barotrauma.

Pearl: plateau ≤ 30 and driving pressure < 15 are equally important. If plateau exceeds 30 at 6 mL/kg, reduce to 5 or 4 mL/kg PBW accepting permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥ 7.20).

Pitfall: raising RR to maintain minute vent → air-trapping, worsens dynamic hyperinflation. Accept CO₂.
ref: ARDS Network. NEJM 2000;342:1301-8

stem: Which single ventilator parameter has the strongest association with ARDS mortality (Amato 2015)?
explanation:
Why driving pressure: Amato NEJM 2015 mediation analysis — ΔP (Pplat − PEEP) was more strongly associated with survival than TV, Pplat, or PEEP alone. Target ΔP < 15 cmH₂O.

Why not others: TV and Pplat are important components, but ΔP combines them with respiratory system compliance — it captures lung stress better; PEEP alone may increase overdistention if driving pressure rises; RR matters for CO₂ clearance, not directly for lung injury.

Pearl: if ΔP > 15, try: lower TV, higher PEEP (if improves compliance), proning, NMB, ECMO.

Pitfall: driving pressure is only valid with PASSIVE patient (no spontaneous effort). In assist modes the reading is contaminated by patient effort — measure after a brief paralysis dose if needed.
ref: Amato MBP et al. NEJM 2015;372:747-55

stem: A severe ARDS patient has P/F 60 on FiO₂ 100 % + PEEP 18 × 4 hours, pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 65. Which criterion best triggers VV-ECMO referral (EOLIA)?
options: P/F < 50 for 3 h or P/F < 80 for 6 h on FiO₂ ≥ 0.8
Only after 7 days of mechanical ventilation
explanation:
Why these EOLIA criteria: P/F < 50 for ≥ 3 h OR P/F < 80 for ≥ 6 h (on FiO₂ ≥ 0.8), OR pH < 7.25 + PaCO₂ ≥ 60 for ≥ 6 h with RR ≤ 35 + Pplat ≤ 32. EOLIA showed 11 % absolute mortality reduction with ECMO (not statistically significant, but Bayesian reanalysis strongly suggests benefit).

Why not others: P/F < 150 is too permissive (many respond to proning); 'any < 100' misses the settings context; 'only after 7 days' is OPPOSITE — refer EARLY (ideally < 7 days of MV).

Pearl: murray score ≥ 3 also triggers ECMO consideration (CESAR). Before ECMO: try prone, NMB, recruitment manoeuvre, optimise PEEP.

Pitfall: late referral — > 7 days of ventilation is a predictor of worse ECMO outcome; transfer centres are busy and transport takes time.
ref: Combes A et al. EOLIA. NEJM 2018;378:1965-75

stem: Early continuous neuromuscular blockade in severe ARDS:
options: Has no mortality benefit in the ROSE trial, but may improve oxygenation and reduce barotrauma in selected patients
Is standard for every intubated patient
explanation:
Why 'no mortality benefit but selectively useful': ACURASYS (NEJM 2010) showed 48 h cisatracurium ↓ 90-day mortality in severe ARDS. ROSE (NEJM 2019) could NOT replicate this — lighter sedation + proning may have evened the field. Consensus: reserve NMB for refractory asynchrony, high Pplat, ECMO patients.

Why not others: ACURASYS alone is no longer definitive; always avoiding misses genuine indications; routine use causes ICU-acquired weakness, prolonged weaning.

Pearl: cisatracurium 15 mg bolus → 37.5 mg/hr × 48 h (ACURASYS protocol). Train-of-four 1-2/4 target. Add appropriate sedation + analgesia (patient is paralysed but may still have awareness — give midazolam + fentanyl).

Pitfall: omitting sedation during NMB = awake-paralysed PTSD. Always sedate deeply first.
ref: NHLBI PETAL Network. ROSE trial. NEJM 2019;380:1997-2008

stem: Corticosteroids in ARDS (DEXA-ARDS 2020) — correct statement:
options: Dexamethasone 20 mg × 5 d then 10 mg × 5 d reduced 60-day mortality in moderate-severe ARDS
Steroids should only be given in COVID ARDS
explanation:
Why dex 20 → 10: DEXA-ARDS (Villar Lancet Respir Med 2020) in moderate-severe ARDS → 60-day mortality 21 vs 36 % (NNT 7), more ventilator-free days. Started within 30 h of ARDS onset.

Why not others: RECOVERY used 6 mg × 10 d for COVID ARDS (also beneficial); 'steroids increase mortality' is from older sepsis/ARDS trials with very high doses; hydrocortisone works for refractory septic shock, not primarily ARDS.

Pearl: start EARLY (within 14 days, ideally < 72 h of ARDS onset). Watch glucose, infection surveillance.

Pitfall: methylprednisolone 'late' ARDS (> 14 days) — NOT supported (LaSRS trial showed harm).
ref: Villar J et al. DEXA-ARDS. Lancet Respir Med 2020;8:267-76

stem: Alveolar recruitment manoeuvres in ARDS:
options: Should be routine in every intubated patient
Caused increased mortality in the ART trial using aggressive escalating PEEP
explanation:
Why ART showed harm: Alveolar Recruitment Trial (JAMA 2017) used aggressive escalating PEEP up to 45 cmH₂O + brief high-pressure inflation. 28-day mortality was INCREASED (55.3 vs 49.3 %), with more barotrauma, pneumothorax, and haemodynamic collapse.

Why not others: 'always improve survival' is wrong (ART); 'routine every patient' is dangerous; '10 min sustained' refers to old technique, abandoned.

Pearl: brief (10-second) recruitment at 35-40 cmH₂O may transiently improve oxygenation but is NOT standard-of-care post-ART. Prone positioning is safer.

Pitfall: aggressive recruitment in hypovolaemic / RV-dysfunction patients → acute RV failure, shock. Always ensure volume resuscitation first + monitor BP throughout.
ref: ART Investigators. Effect of lung recruitment vs lower PEEP strategy. JAMA 2017;318:1335-45

stem: SBP 90, DBP 60. Calculate the MAP:
explanation:
Why 70: MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3 = 60 + 10 = 70. Equivalent formula: (SBP + 2 × DBP)/3 = 70. Valid at HR 60-100; at HR > 120, diastolic weighting changes.

Why not others: 60 = DBP alone; 75 or 80 misapply the formula.

Pearl: arterial-line MAP is the 'true' area-under-curve MAP (not derived). At low HR, cuff and A-line diverge; trust the A-line if the waveform is damped-free (test with fast-flush).

Pitfall: targeting MAP ≥ 65 universally may be wrong — chronic HTN patients often need MAP ≥ 75-80 to maintain renal + cerebral perfusion (SEPSISPAM 2014 trend).
ref: Standard arterial pressure physiology

stem: Adult traumatic brain injury: what is the TARGET cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)?
explanation:
Why 60-70: BTF 4th ed Level IIB — CPP 60-70. Individualise within this range based on autoregulation status (pressure reactivity index, PRx).

Why not others: < 50 → ischaemia; 50-60 edge of safe; 80-100 → increased ARDS risk from fluid loading and vasopressor-induced pulmonary oedema (Robertson 1999).

Pearl: CPP = MAP − ICP. Raise MAP (noradrenaline) first; if ICP is the problem, address it (sedation, osmotherapy, CSF drain, surgery). Don't chase high CPP in the autoregulation-impaired patient — high MAP may paradoxically raise ICP.

Pitfall: saline resuscitation to augment CPP in TBI → hypernatraemia is okay (goal 145-155), hyperchloraemia + AKI is not. Prefer 3 % NaCl bolus for osmotherapy.
ref: Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines 2017

stem: The HR / SBP ratio (shock index) > 1.0 suggests:
explanation:
Why occult shock: normal SI 0.5-0.7. SI > 1.0 identifies patients with physiological derangement before SBP has dropped — crucial in trauma (abdominal haemorrhage), early sepsis, PE. Modified SI = HR/MAP; > 1.3 even more sensitive.

Why not others: normal volume has low SI; elevated SI is not specific to sepsis or tamponade — it is a general shock index.

Pearl: SI > 0.9 in trauma predicts need for MTP activation, mortality. SI > 1.0 postpartum → active haemorrhage until proven otherwise.

Pitfall: β-blocker users have blunted HR response → SI remains falsely normal in shock.
ref: Allgöwer M, Buri C. Schockindex. Dtsch Med Wochenschr 1967

stem: Which parameter best predicts fluid-responsiveness in a passively ventilated patient on controlled mechanical ventilation (TV 8 mL/kg, sinus rhythm, no spontaneous effort)?
explanation:
Why PPV: dynamic preload index — intrathoracic pressure swings during positive-pressure ventilation vary venous return, producing a cyclic change in SV and PP. PPV > 13 % predicts ~ 15 % SV rise after a 500 mL bolus (sensitivity & specificity ~ 90 %).

Why not others: CVP is a poor predictor (Marik 2013 meta-analysis); UO and lactate are endpoints, not predictors.

Pearl: PPV requires regular cardiac rhythm, controlled MV with TV ≥ 8 mL/kg, no spontaneous effort. For spontaneous or AF — use passive leg raise + CO monitor change > 10 %.

Pitfall: in ARDS (low TV 6 mL/kg), PPV sensitivity drops — use the tidal-volume-challenge technique (transient TV to 8 mL/kg for 60 s).
ref: Marik PE et al. CVP and fluid responsiveness. Crit Care Med 2013;41:1774-81

stem: Cardiogenic shock from acute anterior STEMI, SBP 80, pulmonary oedema, lactate 5. Best initial pharmacologic support?
explanation:
Why NE + dobutamine: SOAP-II (NEJM 2010) showed noradrenaline superior to dopamine in cardiogenic shock (lower mortality in subgroup). Dobutamine adds inotropy without the catecholamine cost. OPTIMA-CC supports this combination in cardiogenic shock.

Why not others: dopamine alone → more arrhythmias and mortality; dobutamine alone drops SBP (β2 vasodilation) in a MAP-dependent brain; nitroglycerin drops afterload but worsens hypotension.

Pearl: mechanical support (Impella, VA-ECMO, IABP) early. Revascularise (PCI) the culprit lesion ASAP — CULPRIT-SHOCK showed culprit-only PCI better than multi-vessel in acute shock.

Pitfall: aggressive fluids worsen pulmonary oedema — small, titrated boluses only.
ref: De Backer D et al. SOAP II. NEJM 2010;362:779-89

stem: Refractory vasoplegic shock on noradrenaline 1 μg/kg/min + vasopressin 0.04 U/min. Add which agent?
options: Any of the above may be reasonable — angiotensin II has the most RCT data
explanation:
Why all can work, ATHOS-3 data best for Ang II: ATHOS-3 (NEJM 2017) showed angiotensin II raised MAP in catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock. Methylene blue inhibits iNOS → NO (used in post-CPB vasoplegia, case series, no RCT). Hydroxocobalamin scavenges NO (reports in distributive shock + cyanide toxicity).

Why not individual answers only: each has a niche — the "best" depends on context, availability, and local expertise.

Pearl: escalation sequence in septic shock: NE → add vasopressin → add hydrocortisone → angiotensin II / methylene blue / hydroxocobalamin as rescue.

Pitfall: methylene blue — interferes with pulse oximetry (false low SpO₂), serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic agents.
ref: Khanna A et al. ATHOS-3. NEJM 2017;377:419-30

stem: A patient with CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 3 and HAS-BLED = 2. Best management of atrial fibrillation?
explanation:
Why DOAC: CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2 (men) or ≥ 3 (women) → oral anticoagulation (Class I). DOACs preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF — RE-LY, ROCKET, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE all showed non-inferior stroke prevention + less ICH + no monitoring.

Why not others: aspirin inferior to warfarin for stroke prevention in AF (no longer recommended); 'no antithrombotic' misses the stroke indication; DAPT is for post-stent, not AF.

Pearl: HAS-BLED ≥ 3 is a flag for closer monitoring, NOT a contraindication to anticoagulation — modify reversible factors (BP control, stop NSAIDs, limit alcohol). DOAC with CrCl < 30 — dose-adjust (apixaban 2.5 mg BID; avoid dabigatran).

Pitfall: valvular AF (mitral stenosis, mechanical valve) → WARFARIN only, not DOAC (RE-ALIGN failed).
ref: Hindricks G et al. 2020 ESC AF Guidelines. Eur Heart J 2021

stem: A 72-year-old presents with chest pain. HEART score components. Which component carries the HEAVIEST weight?
options: All components (History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin) are equally weighted 0-2 each
explanation:
Why equal weight: HEART = History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin — each scored 0, 1 or 2 (max 10). No single component dominates.

Bands: ≤ 3 LOW risk (~ 1.7 % 6-week MACE — discharge with cardiology follow-up); 4-6 MODERATE (~ 17 % — admit, serial troponins, ± stress/CTA); ≥ 7 HIGH (~ 50 % — early invasive strategy).

Pearl: HEART outperformed TIMI and GRACE for discharge decisions in ED chest pain (HEART Pathway RCT).

Pitfall: HEART is for undifferentiated chest pain — do NOT apply to confirmed STEMI (manage per STEMI pathway instead).
ref: Six AJ et al. HEART score. Neth Heart J 2008;16:191-6

stem: CURB-65 score of 3 in community-acquired pneumonia suggests:
explanation:
Why severe: CURB-65: 0-1 outpatient (mortality < 3 %) · 2 short inpatient (~ 9 %) · ≥ 3 severe (~ 22 % mortality), admit, strongly consider ICU.

Why not others: outpatient for 0-1 only; short admission for score 2; mild / no antibiotics never applies to confirmed CAP.

Pearl: IDSA/ATS 2019 ICU admission criteria — major (septic shock, mechanical ventilation) OR ≥ 3 minor (RR ≥ 30, P/F ≤ 250, multilobar, confusion, uraemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension requiring fluids).

Pitfall: CURB-65 under-estimates severity in young healthy patients — age is heavily weighted. Combine with PSI (Pneumonia Severity Index) or clinical judgement.
ref: Lim WS et al. CURB-65. Thorax 2003;58:377-82

stem: A patient with cirrhosis has MELD-Na = 25. Approximate 3-month mortality is:
explanation:
Why ~ 20 %: MELD-Na bands (approximate 90-day mortality): < 10 → < 2 % · 10-19 → ~ 6 % · 20-29 → ~ 20 % · 30-39 → ~ 53 % · ≥ 40 → ~ 71 %. Drives UNOS liver transplant priority since Feb 2016.

Why not others: < 2 % only for MELD-Na < 10; 6 % for 10-19; 53 % for 30-39.

Pearl: formula uses bilirubin, INR, creatinine (all clamped ≥ 1.0; Cr capped at 4.0 or set to 4.0 if dialysis ≥ 2×/wk), then adds Na correction. MELD-Na is always ≥ MELD; capped at 40.

Pitfall: MELD does not fully capture risk — portopulmonary hypertension, hepatopulmonary syndrome, acute-on-chronic liver failure add mortality not reflected.
ref: Kim WR et al. MELD-Na. NEJM 2008;359:1018-26

stem: SOFA score of 11 on ICU day 3 vs day 1 score of 4 indicates:
explanation:
Why deterioration: SOFA quantifies organ dysfunction (6 organs × 0-4). Score ≥ 11 → mortality > 80 %; trend (↑ or ↓) over 48 h predicts outcome better than admission score alone (Levy 2003). A rise of > 2 points in 48 h with suspected infection also defines sepsis (Sepsis-3).

Why not others: rising score = worse; day 3 trend is one of the most prognostic numbers in ICU.

Pearl: ΔSOFA on day 1 vs day 3 outperforms APACHE II for outcome prediction in sepsis.

Pitfall: individual organ scores guide therapy — a rising CV score with falling renal might be sepsis + AKI from ATN; rising neuro + stable organs might be new ICH. Look at components.
ref: Vincent JL et al. SOFA score. Intensive Care Med 1996;22:707-10

stem: An NIHSS of 22 in acute stroke indicates:
explanation:
Why severe: NIHSS bands → 0 none · 1-4 minor · 5-15 moderate · 16-20 moderate-to-severe · 21-42 severe. 22 = severe. Higher NIHSS correlates with LVO (large vessel occlusion) → candidate for mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 h (DAWN, DEFUSE-3).

Why not others: 0 for none; 1-4 for minor; moderate is 5-15.

Pearl: for tPA, favour treatment regardless of severity within 4.5 h (ECASS-III, ENCHANTED). For thrombectomy, NIHSS ≥ 6 + ASPECTS ≥ 6 + LVO on imaging.

Pitfall: posterior circulation strokes score falsely LOW on NIHSS (it is heavily anterior-biased). A patient with 'locked-in' may have NIHSS 3 but need thrombectomy.
ref: Brott T et al. NIHSS. Stroke 1989;20:864-70

stem: A 55-year-old man in septic shock with APACHE II of 28 has approximately what ICU mortality?
explanation:
Why ~ 55 %: APACHE II bands → ≤ 4 (~ 4 %) · 5-9 (~ 8 %) · 10-14 (~ 15 %) · 15-19 (~ 25 %) · 20-24 (~ 40 %) · 25-29 (~ 55 %) · 30-34 (~ 73 %) · ≥ 35 (~ 85 %).

Why not others: 15 % is 10-14 band; 40 % is 20-24; 85 % is ≥ 35.

Pearl: APACHE II uses the worst value of each variable in the first 24 h of ICU admission — NOT the admission value. Includes 12 physiologic variables, age, chronic health.

Pitfall: APACHE II is for ICU research and benchmarking — do NOT use it to make individual withdrawal decisions. SOFA trend + patient wishes + clinical judgement guide that.
ref: Knaus WA et al. APACHE II. Crit Care Med 1985;13:818-29

stem: The antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose is:
explanation:
Why NAC: replenishes hepatic glutathione, which conjugates the toxic NAPQI metabolite. Give within 8-10 h for best hepatoprotection; still effective beyond 24 h, especially in massive OD or late presentation (re-dose per levels / INR).

Why not others: flumazenil reverses benzos (seizure risk!); fomepizole for toxic alcohols; naloxone for opioids.

Pearl: 21-hour IV regimen — 150 mg/kg over 60 min → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h (Prescott). Oral 72 h regimen alternative. Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram to decide at 4 h post-ingestion for known timing.

Pitfall: staggered overdose, repeated dosing, or unknown timing — treat empirically; cannot use nomogram.
ref: Prescott LF. NAC for paracetamol poisoning. BMJ 1979;2:1097-100

stem: A patient with calcium-channel-blocker overdose has refractory shock despite calcium, glucagon, and high-dose insulin + dextrose. Next step?
options: Lipid emulsion 20 % 1.5 mL/kg bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min
explanation:
Why lipid emulsion: intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) 20 % creates a plasma lipid sink that sequesters lipophilic drugs (CCB, local anaesthetics, TCA, bupropion). 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min → 0.25 mL/kg/min for 30-60 min.

Why not others: methylene blue is for refractory vasoplegia (methaemoglobinaemia); HD rarely removes CCB (large Vd, lipophilic); vasopressin alone is inadequate at this point.

Pearl: CCB OD escalation: Ca gluconate → high-dose insulin (1 U/kg bolus → 0.5-1 U/kg/hr + dextrose titrated to normoglycaemia) → ILE → methylene blue → VA-ECMO.

Pitfall: insulin resistance in CCB OD is dose-dependent — may need 10 U/kg/hr! Give concentrated dextrose via central line to avoid fluid overload.
ref: Gosselin S et al. Evidence-based recommendations on ILE therapy. Clin Toxicol 2016

stem: A patient on heparin develops major bleeding. Which agent FULLY reverses UFH?
options: Protamine sulphate 1 mg per 100 units heparin given in past 2-3 h
explanation:
Why protamine: cationic peptide that binds anionic heparin → inactive complex. 1 mg protamine per 100 units UFH given in previous 2-3 h, max ~ 50 mg (slow IV, risk of anaphylaxis/pulmonary HTN).

Why not others: vitamin K reverses warfarin (slow — needs factor synthesis); andexanet for apixaban/rivaroxaban; idarucizumab for dabigatran.

Pearl: UFH half-life 60-90 min — if infusion stopped > 3 h ago, protamine not needed. LMWH partial reversal only (~ 60 %) — give 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin within 8 h.

Pitfall: protamine hypersensitivity in patients on NPH insulin, fish allergy, prior vasectomy — slow infusion, premedicate with antihistamine.
ref: Hirsh J et al. ACCP Guidelines. Chest 2008;133:141S-59S

stem: A 30-year-old with opioid overdose has RR 6, pinpoint pupils, SpO₂ 82 %. Initial dose of naloxone?
explanation:
Why low-dose titration: start naloxone 0.04-0.1 mg IV (or 0.4 mg IM if no IV) and titrate q 2-3 min to adequate ventilation (RR ≥ 12, SpO₂ > 92 %). Goal is RESPIRATION, not full wakefulness — avoid acute withdrawal + pulmonary oedema.

Why not others: 4 mg bolus → severe withdrawal, agitation, hypertension, pulmonary oedema; intranasal 4 mg is reasonable pre-hospital; just intubating misses the reversible pathology.

Pearl: naloxone half-life (30-90 min) is SHORTER than most opioids (methadone, fentanyl patch, buprenorphine) → repeat dosing or infusion (2/3 of effective bolus per hour).

Pitfall: single dose then discharge → recurrence. Observe ≥ 6 h (longer for long-acting opioids).
ref: Boyer EW. Management of opioid analgesic overdose. NEJM 2012;367:146-55

stem: Digoxin toxicity with K⁺ 6.2, VT, and refractory shock. Best therapy?
explanation:
Why DigiFab: immune Fab fragments bind digoxin → inactive complex, excreted renally. Rapid onset (< 1 h). Indications — life-threatening arrhythmia, K > 5 in acute OD, serum digoxin > 10 ng/mL acute or > 4 ng/mL chronic, haemodynamic instability.

Why not others: insulin shift is temporising (DigiFab is definitive); HD does NOT remove digoxin (large Vd); β-blocker worsens heart block.

Pearl: dose empirically — 10-20 vials acute OD if amount unknown; 1-2 vials chronic. 1 vial (40 mg) binds 0.5 mg digoxin. In acute OD with K > 5 + arrhythmia: do NOT give calcium (debated — may cause 'stone heart' in digoxin tox).

Pitfall: digoxin level after DigiFab is total (bound + free) — confusing, uninterpretable.
ref: Antman EM et al. Treatment of 150 cases of life-threatening digitalis intoxication with digoxin-specific Fab. Circulation 1990;81:1744-52

stem: A patient with salicylate overdose has pH 7.45, salicylate level 65 mg/dL, tinnitus, confusion. Alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate works because:
options: Traps ionised salicylate out of CNS and in urine (increases elimination)
explanation:
Why alkalinisation works: salicylate (weak acid, pKa 3.5) exists more in its ionised form when pH is high. The ionised form cannot cross the blood-brain barrier (less neurotoxicity) and cannot be reabsorbed in renal tubules (more urinary elimination). Target serum pH 7.45-7.55 and urine pH ≥ 7.5.

Why not others: hypoglycaemia is separate issue; no direct neutralisation; antiemetic unrelated.

Pearl: dose — 150 mEq NaHCO₃ in 1 L D5W at 150-200 mL/hr + KCl (hypoK is common, impairs alkalinisation). HD if level > 100 mg/dL, severe acidosis, mental status change, pulmonary oedema.

Pitfall: intubation DANGER — drop in minute ventilation → sudden acidosis + arrest (same trap as ketoacidosis). Match hyperventilation on vent.
ref: Dargan PI, Wallace CI, Jones AL. An evidence based flowchart to guide the management of acute salicylate (aspirin) overdose. Emerg Med J 2002;19:206-9

stem: Benzodiazepine overdose with CNS depression and respiratory depression. Antidote (flumazenil) is:
options: Contraindicated in co-ingestion or benzo-dependence (seizure risk)
Should be given as 2 mg bolus
explanation:
Why contraindicated in co-ingestion/dependence: flumazenil may precipitate seizures in: chronic benzodiazepine users (withdrawal seizure), mixed OD with pro-convulsants (TCA, cocaine, bupropion), epilepsy, head injury. Status epilepticus triggered by flumazenil is often refractory because benzos no longer work.

Why not others: 'always indicated' wrong; it is NOT equivalent to naloxone (safer because opioid-related seizures are rare); 2 mg is too high (start 0.2 mg).

Pearl: dose — 0.2 mg IV over 15 s, may repeat to total 1-3 mg. Short half-life (~ 50 min) < most benzos → re-sedation possible.

Pitfall: in most ICU/ED benzo OD the right answer is supportive care (airway, ventilation) rather than flumazenil.
ref: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed

stem: A patient with suspected cyanide poisoning (smoke inhalation, altered mentation, lactate 14) has unknown level. Best antidote?
options: Amyl nitrite inhalation + sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulphate (classic kit)
explanation:
Why hydroxocobalamin: binds free cyanide → cyanocobalamin (vit B12), excreted renally. Safe in smoke inhalation victims (does NOT cause methaemoglobinaemia unlike nitrites — dangerous when CO co-exists). Dose 5 g IV over 15 min; repeat once if needed.

Why not others: thiosulphate alone is slow; nitrite kit causes methaemoglobinaemia (reduces O₂-carrying capacity further) — avoid in smoke inhalation; methylene blue is for methaemoglobinaemia.

Pearl: cyanide clues: lactate > 10 after smoke inhalation, metabolic acidosis unresponsive to O₂, bitter almond breath (only 40 % can smell it), 'bright red' venous blood (saturated O₂).

Pitfall: hydroxocobalamin turns urine/skin RED, interferes with pulse oximetry and some lab assays for up to 48 h.
ref: Borron SW et al. Hydroxocobalamin for severe cyanide poisoning. Ann Emerg Med 2007;49:794-801

stem: A patient has a convulsive seizure that has lasted 7 minutes. First-line pharmacotherapy is:
options: Benzodiazepine (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV or midazolam 10 mg IM)
explanation:
Why benzo first: status epilepticus (≥ 5 min) — benzo stops ~ 60-70 % of seizures. Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) if access available; midazolam 10 mg IM (RAMPART trial: superior to IV lorazepam when no line) otherwise.

Why not others: phenytoin/fosphenytoin/levetiracetam/valproate are second-line (after 20-30 min — ESETT trial showed all equivalent); propofol is third-line (refractory SE) after intubation.

Pearl: under-dosing is the commonest error — give FULL weight-based dose first (e.g. 4 mg lorazepam for 40-kg + patient, not 2). May repeat once if seizures continue at 5 min.

Pitfall: 'wait and see' kills neurons. Every 30 min of SE increases mortality and refractoriness. Non-convulsive SE (unexplained coma post-convulsion) needs cEEG.
ref: Glauser T et al. AES Guideline. Epilepsy Curr 2016;16:48-61

stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of the ICH Score?
explanation:
Why not glucose: ICH Score (Hemphill 2001) = GCS (3-4: 2 pts · 5-12: 1 · 13-15: 0) + volume ≥ 30 cm³ (1) + IVH (1) + infratentorial (1) + age ≥ 80 (1). Max 6.

Why the others ARE components: GCS, volume, IVH all score.

Pearl: 30-day mortality bands: 0→0 % · 1→13 % · 2→26 % · 3→72 % · 4→97 % · ≥ 5→100 %. Volume estimation (ABC/2 method) is rapid at bedside.

Pitfall: ICH Score does NOT guide withdrawal — self-fulfilling prophecy. Aggressive BP control (SBP 140, INTERACT-2), reversal of coagulopathy, and early neurosurgical consultation matter.
ref: Hemphill JC et al. ICH Score. Stroke 2001;32:891-7

stem: A patient presents 2 h after acute ischaemic stroke with NIHSS 8. CT shows no bleed, no early ischaemic change. Best next step?
explanation:
Why tPA: within 4.5 h, NINDS and ECASS-III established alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10 % bolus + 90 % infusion over 60 min) for eligible AIS patients. Starting now is time-critical — every 15 min delay = 1 month less disability-free life.

Why not others: MRI delays therapy; aspirin alone misses time window; thrombectomy is for LVO — start tPA concurrently ('bridging') unless contraindicated.

Pearl: tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV single bolus is non-inferior and now preferred at many centres (ACT, AcT, EXTEND-IA TNK).

Pitfall: BP must be < 185/110 before tPA and < 180/105 for 24 h after. Use labetalol/nicardipine. Check glucose (excludes stroke mimic hypoglycaemia).
ref: Powers WJ et al. 2019 AHA/ASA AIS Guidelines (Update 2024)

stem: A SAH patient on day 5 develops new weakness and confusion. TCD shows elevated MCA velocities. Best intervention?
options: Induced hypertension (MAP up to 20-30 % above baseline) + optimise euvolaemia
explanation:
Why induced HTN: delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) from vasospasm typically peaks days 4-14. Modern 'triple-H' is actually single-H — induced hypertension (euvolaemic haemodilution NOT recommended). Raise MAP with noradrenaline until neurologic improvement or MAP ceiling reached.

Why not others: hypothermia no proven benefit in SAH; mannitol for ↑ ICP; decompressive craniectomy for refractory ICP or malignant MCA, not vasospasm per se.

Pearl: prophylactic nimodipine 60 mg PO q 4 h × 21 days — MORTALITY benefit (BRANT 1989). Doesn't prevent spasm but improves outcomes.

Pitfall: aneurysm must be SECURED (clip or coil) before induced HTN; otherwise risk of rebleed is catastrophic.
ref: Connolly ES et al. AHA/ASA SAH Guidelines. Stroke 2012

stem: A TBI patient has ICP 28 despite head elevation, sedation, normothermia, and PaCO₂ 35. Next step?
explanation:
Why osmotherapy: tier-2 after basic measures. Hypertonic saline (3 % — 250 mL or 23.4 % — 30 mL bolus) OR mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg. Both lower ICP within 30 min.

Why not others: hyperventilation to PaCO₂ < 30 → cerebral vasoconstriction, ISCHAEMIA (avoid unless herniation, short bridge); steroids HARMFUL in TBI (CRASH trial, mortality ↑); lowering MAP cuts CPP → ischaemia.

Pearl: hypertonic saline preferred over mannitol in hypovolaemic / hypotensive patients. Target Na 145-155 with repeat boluses. CSF drain via EVD if available.

Pitfall: rebound ICP rise after mannitol — don't use repeatedly if serum osm > 320 or Na > 155.
ref: Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines 2017

stem: A patient has K⁺ 7.0 with ECG showing peaked T waves and widened QRS. First action is:
explanation:
Why calcium first: CARDIAC MEMBRANE STABILISATION — onset 1-3 min. Calcium does NOT lower K⁺ but prevents arrest while you shift it. 10 % Ca gluconate 10-30 mL IV over 10 min (peripheral) OR 10 % Ca chloride 10 mL (central — more elemental Ca but tissue necrosis risk peripherally).

Why not others: insulin + dextrose (SHIFT, 20 min onset) comes next; salbutamol (shift, 30 min, additive); furosemide / dialysis REMOVES K⁺ (slower) — essential but after stabilisation.

Pearl: ECG severity order — peaked T → prolonged PR → widened QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole. Sine wave = pre-arrest, do EVERYTHING simultaneously.

Pitfall: in digoxin toxicity, calcium is controversial (some advocate; traditional teaching 'stone heart'). Use DigiFab instead.
ref: Kraft MD et al. Treatment of electrolyte disorders. AJHP 2005

stem: A chronic alcoholic has serum Na 112 with severe lethargy and seizures. Over what rate should sodium be corrected in the first 24 hours to minimise osmotic demyelination?
options: 4-6 mEq/L rise in first 4-6 h, total ≤ 8 mEq/L in 24 h
explanation:
Why 4-6 then cap at 8: severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) — rapid 4-6 mEq/L rise resolves cerebral oedema (3 % NaCl 150 mL bolus × 2-3 or infusion). AFTER symptom resolution limit TOTAL 24-h rise to ≤ 8 mEq/L (≤ 6 in high-risk: alcoholic, malnourished, hepatic, chronic hypo-K).

Why not others: 'to 135 in 6 h' = osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS); 15 mEq/L exceeds safe limit; bolus-only without a target → overshoot.

Pearl: OVERSHOOT rescue — if Na rises too fast, LOWER it back with 5 % dextrose infusion ± DDAVP 2-4 μg (reverses free water loss).

Pitfall: ODS presents 2-6 days AFTER correction (dysarthria, dysphagia, para/quadriparesis) — too late. Prevention is the only treatment.
ref: Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma sodium. NEJM 2015;372:55-65

stem: A patient on furosemide has K 2.4, Mg 1.0. Best replacement strategy?
options: K and Mg can be given together
explanation:
Why Mg first: hypomagnesaemia causes renal K wasting — you cannot retain K until Mg is normalised. Mg deficit ALSO prolongs QT, causes torsades, impairs PTH secretion (hypoCa).

Why not others: K first + Mg low → K pees out, no gain; combined is pragmatic but Mg-first is the teaching principle; ignoring Mg is wrong.

Pearl: Mg sulphate 2-4 g IV over 30-60 min (slower: hypotension, flushing). Target serum Mg 1.8-2.5. Replete PO₄ too if low — depleted at the same time.

Pitfall: rapid IV Mg → bradycardia, respiratory depression; watch deep tendon reflexes in myasthenia.
ref: Kraft MD et al. AJHP 2005

stem: Acute severe hypercalcaemia (Ca 14 mg/dL, altered mentation). First-line therapy?
options: Normal saline 200-300 mL/hr + calcitonin 4 U/kg SC + IV bisphosphonate
explanation:
Why combined approach: hypercalcaemic crisis — isotonic saline (dehydration from calcium-driven polyuria, 2-4 L/24 h) + calcitonin 4 U/kg SC q 6-12 h (fastest onset, 2-6 h, tachyphylaxis by 48 h) + IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg or pamidronate 60-90 mg — onset 2-4 days, durable).

Why not others: bisphosphonate alone — slow onset; calcitonin alone — short duration; steroid only works for granulomatous or malignancy-related (lymphoma).

Pearl: dialysis for Ca > 18, refractory. Avoid loop diuretics UNLESS fluid overloaded (old 'forced saline diuresis' — actually worsens Ca).

Pitfall: look for the cause — PTH (primary hyperparathyroidism), malignancy (PTHrP), vit D, immobility, drugs (lithium, thiazides).
ref: Minisola S et al. The diagnosis and management of hypercalcaemia. BMJ 2015;350:h2723

stem: Hypophosphataemia in a critically ill patient (PO₄ 0.8 mg/dL). Clinical consequences include:
options: Respiratory muscle weakness, failure to wean
explanation:
Why 'all': PO₄ is central to ATP and 2,3-DPG. Deficiency causes diaphragmatic weakness (wean failure), left-shifted O₂-Hb curve, RBC fragility, rhabdomyolysis, impaired myocardial contractility.

Why not others alone: each is correct but incomplete.

Pearl: replete IV — K-phos or Na-phos 15-30 mmol over 4-6 h if PO₄ < 1.0 and symptomatic; PO (Neutra-Phos, phos Sandoz) if stable. Max IV rate 7.5 mmol/hr.

Pitfall: refeeding syndrome — insulin-driven intracellular PO₄, Mg, K shift. Replete BEFORE starting feeds in at-risk patients, re-check q 12 h × 72 h.
ref: Geerse DA et al. Treatment of hypophosphataemia in the ICU. Crit Care 2010;14:R147

stem: Shockable rhythm cardiac arrest. Initial defibrillation energy for a biphasic defibrillator:
explanation:
Why 120-200 J biphasic: biphasic defibs are more efficient — 150-200 J first shock is standard. Monophasic (old) = 360 J. Device manufacturer labels the first-dose energy — follow it.

Why not others: monophasic equivalent is outdated; 360 J biphasic is excessive and not evidence-based; starting at max unnecessarily shocks.

Pearl: second and subsequent shocks at same or escalating energy per device. Minimise peri-shock pauses (resume compressions IMMEDIATELY). Do not over-interpret rhythm during CPR.

Pitfall: 'look at monitor' pause > 10 s — pure harm. Use capnography for rhythm check.
ref: AHA ACLS 2020 Guidelines

stem: Adrenaline (epinephrine) dose in adult cardiac arrest:
explanation:
Why 1 mg q 3-5 min: standard ACLS dose 1 mg IV/IO (or dilute to 10 mL, flush), repeat q 3-5 min during arrest. Give IMMEDIATELY after confirming non-shockable (asystole/PEA); after 2nd shock in shockable (VF/pVT).

Why not others: 0.3 mg IM is anaphylaxis dose; 0.1 mg is bradycardia / pre-arrest push-dose; 10 mg is not used.

Pearl: PARAMEDIC-2 (NEJM 2018) — epinephrine ↑ ROSC but outcomes beyond ROSC are modest + more severe neurologic deficit survivors. Still standard of care.

Pitfall: epinephrine via peripheral IV — give in free-flowing line with flush; avoid distal hand veins.
ref: AHA ACLS 2020 Guidelines

stem: A patient in refractory VF after 3 shocks. Next drug?
explanation:
Why amiodarone: ALIVE trial — amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus (then 150 mg if persistent) for shock-refractory VF/pVT. Preferred antiarrhythmic in ACLS.

Why not others: lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg is alternative (if amiodarone unavailable; some evidence equivalent — ALPS trial); Mg for torsades or hypoMg; atropine for bradycardia (removed from asystole/PEA algorithm 2010).

Pearl: 'drug-shock-drug-shock' sequence with quality CPR > drug choice. Address reversible causes (H's and T's) throughout.

Pitfall: amiodarone infiltration → severe tissue necrosis. Use central or large peripheral line with flush.
ref: Kudenchuk PJ et al. ALPS trial. NEJM 2016;374:1711-22

stem: Post-ROSC management of a comatose patient: target temperature per 2021 ILCOR?
options: Normothermia with active prevention of fever (TTM target 36-37.5 °C)
explanation:
Why 36-37.5 °C + fever prevention: TTM-2 (NEJM 2021) showed no benefit of 33 °C vs normothermia; ILCOR 2022 updated recommendation — target 36-37.5 °C with active fever prevention (< 37.7 °C) for ≥ 72 h after arrest.

Why not others: hyperthermia worsens outcomes; mandatory 32 °C is outdated; no control allows fever → secondary brain injury.

Pearl: other post-ROSC pillars — SBP ≥ 90 / MAP ≥ 65 (consider ≥ 80 to maintain CPP), SpO₂ 94-98 % (avoid hyperoxia), PaCO₂ 35-45, glucose 7.8-10 mmol/L, treat underlying cause (PCI for cardiac).

Pitfall: premature neuro-prognostication — wait ≥ 72 h off sedation; combine clinical, EEG, imaging, biomarkers (NSE).
ref: Dankiewicz J et al. TTM-2. NEJM 2021;384:2283-94

stem: PEA arrest in a trauma patient — most likely reversible cause to address IMMEDIATELY at the bedside?
explanation:
Why tension pneumo: in trauma PEA, mechanical causes dominate — tension pneumo and tamponade kill in minutes. Bilateral finger/needle thoracostomies take seconds and are often diagnostic + therapeutic.

Why not others: hypoxia is reversible — but requires airway; tamponade important (ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis / clamshell) — second priority; hypothermia unlikely in acute trauma arrest.

Pearl: 'HOTT' trauma arrest algorithm — Hypoxia (secure airway), Oxygenate (ventilate), Tension pneumo (decompress bilaterally), Tamponade (pericardiocentesis / clamshell). All within 60 s.

Pitfall: standard ACLS epinephrine in traumatic arrest — controversial, may worsen bleeding. Focus on reversible causes and MTP.
ref: ATLS 10th ed · Lockey DJ et al. Trauma arrest. Resuscitation 2013;84:722-5

stem: STEMI door-to-balloon (D2B) target for primary PCI?
explanation:
Why < 90 min: ACC/AHA + ESC — D2B ≤ 90 min for PCI-capable hospitals; FMC-to-device ≤ 120 min for transferred patients. Every 30 min delay = 7.5 % relative mortality increase.

Why not others: < 30 is aspirational, rare; < 60 is for shock, best-performing centres; 180 is too long.

Pearl: if PCI not available < 120 min FMC → give fibrinolytic (tenecteplase weight-based) within 30 min and transfer. Rescue PCI if failed reperfusion.

Pitfall: aspirin 162-325 mg chewed + loading ADP blocker (ticagrelor 180 mg, prasugrel 60 mg — NOT in > 75 yr / prior stroke, clopidogrel 600 mg) + anticoagulation (UFH or enoxaparin).
ref: O'Gara PT et al. 2013 ACCF/AHA STEMI Guidelines

stem: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema, SBP 155, SpO₂ 86 %. First-line therapy?
explanation:
Why diuretic + nitrate + NIV: furosemide IV 40-80 mg (or 2.5 × usual oral dose) + GTN infusion 10-200 μg/min (preload reduction) + CPAP/BiPAP — the 3-NO triad reduces intubation and mortality.

Why not others: intubation → may be needed if NIV failing but try NIV first; saline worsens oedema; dopamine → no survival benefit, more arrhythmias.

Pearl: DOSE trial — bolus vs infusion of furosemide equivalent. Diuretic + vasodilator synergistic in hypertensive AHF. Consider CPAP over BiPAP in pure CHF.

Pitfall: ACE-I/ARB/ARNI — continue outpatient; initiate on day of discharge for new HF (IMPACT-HF).
ref: Masip J et al. Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care 2018

stem: Unstable AF with rapid ventricular response, SBP 85, chest pain. Best management?
explanation:
Why cardioversion: HAEMODYNAMIC INSTABILITY (hypotension, ischaemia, HF) with tachyarrhythmia — synchronised DC cardioversion is first-line regardless of rhythm. 120-200 J biphasic for AF, 100 J for flutter/SVT.

Why not others: β-blocker and CCB worsen hypotension; amiodarone is for rate control / chemical conversion in stable patients (slow onset).

Pearl: sedate (etomidate / propofol / ketamine) before shock. Pre-shock amiodarone 300 mg if cardioversion likely to fail (ventricular ectopy).

Pitfall: AF > 48 h duration + no anticoagulation → thromboembolism risk with cardioversion. But in unstable patient, prioritise haemodynamics; give heparin + then cardiovert.
ref: Hindricks G et al. 2020 ESC AF Guidelines

stem: Cardiogenic shock from MI unresponsive to vasopressors + dobutamine, lactate rising. Next step?
options: Mechanical circulatory support (Impella, IABP, or VA-ECMO)
explanation:
Why MCS: refractory cardiogenic shock (SCAI stage D-E) — early MCS insertion improves outcomes vs continued medical therapy. Options: IABP (modest afterload reduction, familiar), Impella (active LV unloading), VA-ECMO (complete biventricular support ± oxygenation).

Why not others: adding inotropes escalates oxygen demand, worsens ischaemia; diuretic in hypoperfusion → renal failure.

Pearl: ECMO-CS / ECLS-SHOCK trials — results mixed for VA-ECMO in CS; outcomes depend on patient selection, team expertise, and complication management.

Pitfall: IABP-SHOCK II (NEJM 2012) — IABP alone no mortality benefit in AMI shock. Many centres now favour Impella or VA-ECMO.
ref: Thiele H et al. IABP-SHOCK II. NEJM 2012;367:1287-96

stem: A patient with massive PE (SBP 70, lactate 6, RV dysfunction on echo). Best treatment?
options: Wait for CT angiogram before treating
explanation:
Why systemic tPA: massive PE (haemodynamic instability) — class I indication per ESC + AHA. Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 h OR 50 mg bolus in cardiac arrest. Mortality benefit established.

Why not others: heparin alone insufficient in massive PE; observation kills; CT is usually unnecessary if bedside echo shows RV dilation/strain in a crashing patient.

Pearl: submassive PE (RV dysfunction + biomarkers, normotensive) — risk-benefit; consider catheter-directed thrombolysis (EKOS, ULTIMA).

Pitfall: contraindications — recent ICH, stroke < 3 mo, active bleeding. ECMO or surgical embolectomy as rescue.
ref: Konstantinides SV et al. 2019 ESC PE Guidelines

stem: Empiric antibiotics for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in a 50-year-old?
explanation:
Why combo + dex: vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q 8-12 h + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q 12 h covers S. pneumoniae (incl. resistant), N. meningitidis, H. influenzae. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV q 6 h × 4 d given WITH or BEFORE antibiotics — reduces death + neurologic sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis (de Gans 2002).

Why not others: vanco alone misses gram-negatives; mero alone is reasonable but ceftriaxone better for strep; pip-tazo doesn't cover intracellular organisms + poor CSF.

Pearl: age > 50 / immunocompromised / alcoholic → ADD ampicillin 2 g q 4 h for Listeria. Add acyclovir if HSV suspected.

Pitfall: never delay antibiotics for LP — do CT if focal neuro / papilloedema / age > 60, otherwise LP first. Start abx + dex empirically.
ref: Tunkel AR et al. IDSA Bacterial Meningitis Guidelines. Clin Infect Dis 2004

stem: HAP/VAP suspected Pseudomonas and MRSA. Best empiric regimen?
options: Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam + a second antipseudomonal (e.g. aminoglycoside OR fluoroquinolone)
explanation:
Why double antipseudomonal + MRSA cover: IDSA/ATS 2016 HAP/VAP guidelines — if septic, structurally abnormal lung, or risk factors for resistance, use double antipseudomonal (β-lactam + aminoglycoside OR fluoroquinolone) + MRSA agent (vanco OR linezolid).

Why not others: vanco + cefepime single-coverage; ceftriaxone + azithro is CAP regimen; linezolid alone misses gram-neg.

Pearl: de-escalate within 48-72 h based on cultures. Typical duration 7 days (not 14) per PneumA trial.

Pitfall: aminoglycoside monotherapy for gram-neg — never (poor lung penetration, risk/benefit unfavourable).
ref: Kalil AC et al. IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP 2016

stem: First-line treatment for Clostridioides difficile severe colitis (WBC 15, Cr 1.6)?
options: Oral vancomycin 125 mg PO q 6 h
Oral fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID (preferred by IDSA 2021)
explanation:
Why either vanco OR fidaxomicin: IDSA 2021 — fidaxomicin is NOW PREFERRED (fewer recurrences); oral vancomycin is acceptable, cheaper, equally effective for initial cure. Dose: vanco 125 mg PO q 6 h × 10 d; fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID × 10 d.

Why not metronidazole: no longer first-line (inferior cure rates — Johnson 2014); reserve for mild cases when vanco/fidaxomicin unavailable.

Pearl: fulminant (ileus, hypotension, toxic megacolon) → oral vanco 500 mg q 6 h ± rectal vanco + IV metronidazole. Surgery consult for colectomy.

Pitfall: stopping PPI, offending antibiotic, and antidiarrhoeal (loperamide — DANGEROUS, can precipitate toxic megacolon).
ref: Johnson S et al. IDSA 2021 CDI Clinical Practice Guidelines

stem: Vancomycin target in serious MRSA infection (bacteraemia, endocarditis, meningitis)?
explanation:
Why trough 15-20 / AUC 400-600: ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP 2020 — AUC-guided dosing is preferred (lower AKI risk); trough 15-20 is the older surrogate. Target ratio AUC/MIC ≥ 400.

Why not others: trough 5-10 insufficient for serious MRSA; 10-15 for non-serious infection (cellulitis); peak is not typically monitored.

Pearl: load 25-30 mg/kg (actual BW), maintenance 15-20 mg/kg q 8-12 h. In CRRT, loading unchanged, maintenance reduced + TDM.

Pitfall: nephrotoxicity rises above AUC 650. Monitor daily Cr. Use ideal BW if BMI > 30 to avoid overdosing.
ref: Rybak MJ et al. ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP 2020 Vancomycin Consensus Guideline

stem: A septic patient on piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin develops AKI (Cr 1.0 → 2.3). Best approach?
options: Switch pip-tazo to cefepime; continue vanco with dose adjustment + TDM
explanation:
Why switch pip-tazo: several studies suggest the vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam combination is synergistically nephrotoxic (vs vanco + cefepime or vanco + meropenem). Switching the β-lactam often stabilises Cr.

Why not others: continuing worsens AKI; stopping vanco uncovers MRSA; mero is OK but pip-tazo swap to cefepime is first move.

Pearl: re-check urine output, hydration, co-administered nephrotoxins (contrast, NSAIDs, loops). Check vanco trough / AUC — reduce dose.

Pitfall: ongoing fluid resus with saline → hyperchloraemia + AKI. Switch to balanced crystalloid.
ref: Luther MK et al. Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam and AKI. Crit Care Med 2018;46:12-20

stem: KDIGO-recommended effluent dose for CRRT?
explanation:
Why 20-25: KDIGO 2012 recommends DELIVERED effluent 20-25 mL/kg/hr. Prescribe 25-30 to account for 10-20 % downtime (filter changes, procedures). Higher doses (RENAL + ATN trials) did not improve outcomes.

Why not others: 10-15 too low; 40-45 reserved for specific indications (severe hyperammonaemia, intoxication); 60 is 'high-volume' — no mortality benefit in septic AKI.

Pearl: if raising intensity for intoxication (e.g. methanol) — adjust antibiotic doses UP accordingly (see CRRT antibiotic table).

Pitfall: prescribing dose vs delivered dose — audit. Filter clotting, port issues, and transport reduce delivered dose below prescription.
ref: KDIGO AKI Guideline 2012 · RENAL + ATN NEJM

stem: Patient on CRRT with regional citrate anticoagulation develops iCa (systemic) 0.95 mmol/L, total Ca 2.5 mmol/L, metabolic acidosis. Likely cause?
explanation:
Why citrate accumulation: ratio total:ionised Ca > 2.5 indicates citrate not being metabolised (liver failure, severe shock). Causes paradoxical hypocalcaemia (bound), metabolic acidosis (citrate is a bicarb precursor normally but accumulates as unmetabolised acid).

Why not others: insufficient citrate → clots the circuit; hyperK and hypoPO₄ don't explain this pattern.

Pearl: response — reduce citrate infusion rate; consider switching to heparin or no anticoagulation; treat underlying shock / hepatic failure.

Pitfall: continuing citrate in severe liver failure / profound shock → worsening acidosis + citrate toxicity. Monitor total:ionised Ca q 6 h in high-risk patients.
ref: Oudemans-van Straaten HM et al. Citrate anticoagulation for CRRT. Crit Care 2012

stem: Severe rhabdomyolysis (CK 50 000, Cr rising, K 6.0, anuria). Role of CRRT?
options: Indicated for AKI complications (K, volume, uraemia), NOT to remove myoglobin
explanation:
Why for AKI complications: standard dialyser pores do NOT clear myoglobin (17 kDa). CRRT is indicated for the usual AKI reasons — refractory K, volume overload, severe acidosis, uraemia.

Why not others: myoglobin removal requires high-cut-off / high-flux filters (specialised); contraindicated — wrong; fluids are still cornerstone (aim UO > 200-300 mL/hr pre-CRRT).

Pearl: early aggressive isotonic fluid (NS or Ringer's; avoid lactate in severe hyperK) 1-2 L/hr titrated to UO. Alkalinise urine with bicarbonate if feasible (trap myoglobin as less toxic form).

Pitfall: compartment syndrome — the mechanical cause. Surgical fasciotomy may be needed concurrently.
ref: Bosch X et al. Rhabdomyolysis and AKI. NEJM 2009;361:62-72

stem: STARRT-AKI trial (2020) conclusion on timing of CRRT initiation?
options: Early vs standard initiation shows NO mortality difference
explanation:
Why no mortality difference: STARRT-AKI (NEJM 2020) — 'accelerated' vs 'standard' CRRT initiation in severe AKI showed similar 90-day mortality and more adverse events (hypotension, hypo-PO₄) in early group. Supports standard/delayed strategy guided by refractory K, volume overload, acidosis, uraemia.

Why not others: early benefit not shown; waiting for anuria too long; 'never delay' ignores evidence.

Pearl: initiate CRRT for refractory hyperK, acidosis, volume overload, uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy), OR dialysable intoxication.

Pitfall: initiating in an unstable, under-resuscitated patient → haemodynamic collapse. Resuscitate first, then CRRT.
ref: STARRT-AKI Investigators. NEJM 2020;383:240-51

stem: Stroke patient presents 3 h after symptom onset, NIHSS 10, no ICH on CT, BP 190/100. Best next step?
options: Lower BP < 185/110, then give IV tPA
explanation:
Why lower BP first: tPA contraindication — BP ≥ 185/110 or BP that cannot be lowered. Give labetalol 10-20 mg IV or nicardipine 5 mg/hr. Once BP < 185/110, give tPA. After tPA, keep BP < 180/105 × 24 h.

Why not others: giving tPA with high BP → ICH risk; observation wastes window; aspirin suboptimal if tPA-eligible.

Pearl: tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg bolus is an increasingly preferred alternative.

Pitfall: aggressive BP control (> 25 % drop) can worsen penumbra. Target just below 185/110.
ref: Powers WJ et al. AHA/ASA AIS Guidelines

stem: STEMI patient, PCI not available for 3 h. Best fibrinolytic?
explanation:
Why tenecteplase: single bolus (30-50 mg weight-banded) over 5 s — fewer errors, as effective as accelerated alteplase (ASSENT-2, equivalent 30-day mortality), less non-ICH bleeding. First-line in guidelines where available.

Why not others: streptokinase has more bleeding + allergy; alteplase accelerated is acceptable but requires infusion pumps; reteplase is 2 bolus doses (older).

Pearl: give adjunct — aspirin 162-325 mg chewed + clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg if ≥ 75 yrs) + enoxaparin 30 mg IV + 1 mg/kg SC (reduce in elderly). Transfer for rescue/elective PCI within 24 h.

Pitfall: STREAM — halve TNK dose if age ≥ 75 yrs (reduces ICH).
ref: Armstrong PW et al. STREAM. NEJM 2013;368:1379-87

stem: Which is NOT an ABSOLUTE contraindication to IV thrombolysis in acute stroke?
explanation:
Why age > 80 is RELATIVE: AHA/ASA 2019 — age > 80 is NOT an absolute contraindication (within 0-3 h); still eligible if other criteria met. ECASS-III excluded > 80 yr for 3-4.5 h window, but IST-3 and subsequent trials show benefit.

Why others ARE absolute: previous ICH (lifelong), active bleeding, extensive early infarct (> 1/3 MCA) = bleeding risk + futility.

Pearl: other absolutes — head trauma / stroke in 3 mo, aortic dissection, platelets < 100, INR > 1.7 or DOAC in 48 h, glucose < 50, SBP > 185 / DBP > 110 refractory.

Pitfall: 'awake-up' or unknown onset-time strokes may still qualify with MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch (WAKE-UP trial).
ref: Powers WJ et al. AHA/ASA 2019 (Update 2024)

stem: Hb threshold for PRBC transfusion in a stable ICU patient without active bleeding?
explanation:
Why Hb < 7: restrictive strategy (TRICC, TRISS, TITRe-2) non-inferior or superior to liberal in critically ill, septic, cardiac surgery patients. Transfuse single unit, reassess.

Why not others: Hb < 10 is liberal (higher mortality in TRICC subgroup); 9 is intermediate; symptoms-only ignores objective trigger.

Pearl: exceptions — ACS use Hb < 8-9 (MINT trial); active bleeding — clinical judgment; chronic HF — individualise.

Pitfall: 1 unit = ~ 1 g/dL rise. Order one unit at a time in non-bleeding patients to avoid over-transfusion.
ref: Hébert PC et al. TRICC. NEJM 1999;340:409-17

stem: A patient becomes hypoxic 2 h into a PRBC transfusion. SBP 90, pink frothy sputum, CXR bilateral infiltrates, BNP normal. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Why TRALI: onset < 6 h post-transfusion, hypotension (often — classic feature), non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, BNP normal, no response to diuretics. Donor anti-HLA/granulocyte antibodies attack recipient neutrophils → capillary leak.

Why not TACO: TACO has HYPERTENSION, elevated BNP, responds to diuretics, often older/cardiac.

Why not others: allergic reaction causes urticaria/wheeze (anaphylaxis); haemolytic causes fever, back pain, red urine.

Pearl: management — supportive, lung-protective ventilation; report to blood bank for donor investigation; often male donors or female multiparas.

Pitfall: diuresing TRALI (mistaking for TACO) — worsens shock.
ref: Vlaar APJ et al. ISBT 2019 TRALI redefinition

stem: MTP ratio for trauma haemorrhage per PROPPR?
explanation:
Why 1:1:1: PROPPR (JAMA 2015) — 1:1:1 (plasma:platelet:PRBC) led to faster haemostasis and fewer deaths from exsanguination vs 1:1:2.

Why not others: PRBC alone dilutes clotting factors; platelet-heavy ratios not tested.

Pearl: give TXA 1 g IV over 10 min + 1 g over 8 h within 3 h of trauma (CRASH-2). Fibrinogen < 1.5 g/L → cryoprecipitate 10 units or fibrinogen concentrate. Calcium 1 g per 4 units blood (citrate chelation).

Pitfall: whole blood (where available) is becoming the trauma standard (pre-hospital, military).
ref: Holcomb JB et al. PROPPR. JAMA 2015;313:471-82

stem: Pre-eclampsia with severe features: BP 170/115, headache, proteinuria. First-line antihypertensive?
options: IV labetalol 20 mg or IV hydralazine 5-10 mg OR oral nifedipine 10 mg
explanation:
Why labetalol/hydralazine/nifedipine: target SBP < 160 and DBP < 110 within 30-60 min. Labetalol 20 mg IV (then double q 10 min to max 80, then infusion); hydralazine 5-10 mg IV (reflex tachycardia); nifedipine 10 mg PO.

Why not others: nitroprusside — cyanide toxicity to fetus; ACEi contraindicated in pregnancy; diuretic worsens placental perfusion.

Pearl: magnesium sulphate 4-6 g IV load → 1-2 g/hr for seizure prophylaxis. Delivery is the definitive treatment.

Pitfall: rapid BP drop → placental hypoperfusion. Aim gradual reduction over 30-60 min to SBP ~ 140-150.
ref: ACOG Practice Bulletin 222. Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia 2020

stem: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) — most common cause?
explanation:
Why atony: 70-80 % of PPH. 4 T's — Tone (atony), Trauma (lacerations), Tissue (retained products), Thrombin (coagulopathy).

Why not others: all occur but less frequently; atony is first to treat empirically with bimanual massage + uterotonics.

Pearl: uterotonic ladder — oxytocin 10 U IM / 40 U in 1 L crystalloid, then ergometrine 0.2 mg IM (avoid in HTN), then carboprost 250 μg IM q 15 min (max 8), misoprostol 800-1000 μg PR. Balloon tamponade (Bakri) if medical fails. Surgical options — B-Lynch, hysterectomy.

Pitfall: underestimating blood loss — visual estimate is notoriously inaccurate. Weigh pads/sponges. Activate MTP early.
ref: ACOG Practice Bulletin 183. Postpartum Hemorrhage 2017

stem: A labouring patient suddenly collapses with hypotension, hypoxia, coagulopathy and cardiovascular arrest. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Why AFE: rare (~ 1 in 20 000 deliveries) but catastrophic — sudden hypotension + hypoxia + DIC in labour/early postpartum. Mortality 20-60 %.

Why not others: VAE is usually iatrogenic or trauma; PE less abrupt, less DIC; eclampsia starts with seizures and hypertension.

Pearl: treatment is SUPPORTIVE — intubate, fluids, vasopressors, fix coagulopathy (massive transfusion). Perimortem C-section within 4-5 min if arrest and > 20 weeks (improves maternal AND fetal survival).

Pitfall: clinical diagnosis — no reliable test. Don't delay resuscitation to prove diagnosis.
ref: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. AFE Clinical Guidelines. AJOG 2016

stem: Parkland formula for 70 kg adult with 40 % TBSA burn — total 24-h fluid?
explanation:
Why 11 200: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA = 4 × 70 × 40 = 11 200 mL Lactated Ringer's over 24 h. HALF (5 600 mL) in first 8 h from time of burn, rest over 16 h.

Why not others: 5 600 is just the first 8 h; 8 400 incorrect formula; 20 000 overdoses.

Pearl: titrate to urine output 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr (1-1.5 if myoglobinuria / electrical burn). Be prepared to overshoot (fluid creep) or undershoot (inhalation injury raises needs).

Pitfall: count only 2nd + 3rd degree burns (not superficial). ABA burn-centre transfer for > 10 % TBSA partial, any face/hands/feet/genitals, inhalation, electrical/chemical, trauma, children.
ref: Baxter CR, Shires GT. Parkland Formula. Ann NY Acad Sci 1968

stem: Suspected inhalation injury (singed nasal hairs, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness). Best early action?
explanation:
Why early intubation: airway oedema from thermal/chemical injury worsens in first 24 h — wait too long and intubation becomes impossible. Intubate early even if not yet in respiratory distress.

Why not others: ABG lags behind clinical signs; nebuliser alone misses airway swelling; O₂ via mask misses impending airway obstruction.

Pearl: all patients with facial burns + enclosed-space fire — give 100 % O₂ (treats CO + buys time); check COHb (symptoms > 15 %, severe > 25 %), consider cyanide (hydroxocobalamin 5 g if lactate > 10).

Pitfall: succinylcholine is SAFE in the first 24 h after burn, but becomes dangerous (hyperkalaemia) from ~ 48 h onward through healed phase — use rocuronium.
ref: Walker PF et al. Inhalation injury review. Crit Care 2015;19:351

stem: A 30-year-old with 55 % TBSA burns. Nutrition target?
options: 1.5-2 g/kg/day protein, hypercaloric EN started < 24 h
explanation:
Why high-protein, early EN: severe burns are the most hypermetabolic state. ASPEN/SCCM — early EN < 24-48 h, protein 1.5-2.0 g/kg/day (up to 2.5 in paediatric), kcal 25-30 × stress factor (up to 1.8 in burns > 40 %).
