Why not others: 1 g/kg insufficient; low-calorie worsens catabolism; NPO loses the early EN window.

Pearl: watch for refeeding — replete K, Mg, PO₄ first in malnourished. Oxandrolone / propranolol modulate hypermetabolism in long-stay burns (BURNS 2015).

Pitfall: gastroparesis is common — place NJ tube if gastric intolerance. Monitor bowel sounds + residuals.
ref: McClave SA et al. ASPEN/SCCM Nutrition Guidelines. JPEN 2016

stem: Permissive hypotension in trauma (prior to haemorrhage control) targets:
options: SBP 90-100 in blunt, 80-90 in penetrating (no TBI)
explanation:
Why these targets: damage-control resuscitation — accept lower BP to avoid clot disruption and dilutional coagulopathy before surgical control. SBP ~ 90 in blunt trauma, ~ 80 in penetrating trauma without TBI.

Why not others: normotensive resuscitation pre-haemostasis → more rebleeding and mortality (early aggressive crystalloid worsens outcomes); SBP 70 → under-perfusion of vital organs; TBI requires higher pressures.

Pearl: TBI target SBP ≥ 100 (age 50-69) OR ≥ 110 (age < 50 / ≥ 70) — avoid secondary brain injury.

Pitfall: permissive hypotension is a TEMPORARY bridge to surgical control — not a lasting strategy.
ref: Holcomb JB. Damage-control resuscitation. J Trauma 2007

stem: Tranexamic acid (TXA) in major trauma — timing?
explanation:
Why < 3 h: CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010) — TXA 1 g IV over 10 min + 1 g over 8 h within 3 h reduces all-cause and bleeding mortality. Beyond 3 h — may INCREASE mortality.

Why not others: < 1 h is aspirational; 24 h too late; 'not useful' wrong.

Pearl: CRASH-3 — TXA in TBI < 3 h reduces head-injury mortality (modest). WOMAN trial — TXA in PPH reduces maternal death. HALT-IT (2020) — TXA for GI bleed NO benefit + more VTE.

Pitfall: tubing + saline flush — give through separate line, not with blood products (can clot).
ref: CRASH-2 Trial Collaborators. Lancet 2010;376:23-32

stem: Tension pneumothorax recognition in a hypotensive trauma patient — best immediate action?
options: Immediate needle (14 G) or finger thoracostomy in affected hemithorax
explanation:
Why immediate decompression: tension pneumo is a CLINICAL diagnosis — hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation (late), hypotension. Treatment precedes imaging. 2nd ICS mid-clavicular or 4th-5th ICS mid-axillary (preferred, more reliable).

Why not others: imaging DELAYS treatment; observation kills.

Pearl: after decompression — definitive chest tube (28-32 F).

Pitfall: needle may fail if chest wall thick (trauma, obesity). Finger thoracostomy (open incision + sweep) is more reliable.
ref: ATLS 10th ed

stem: DKA — initial potassium management when K is 3.5 mEq/L before insulin start?
options: Hold insulin + replace K (20-40 mEq/L in IVF) until K > 3.3
explanation:
Why hold insulin until K up: insulin drives K intracellularly → sudden severe hypokalaemia → arrest. Hold insulin if K < 3.3, replete to > 3.3 first, then start insulin. If K 3.3-5.2, start insulin AND concurrent K replacement.

Why not others: starting insulin at K 3.5 is risky — may drop further rapidly; bolus K central only; K at end delays insulin unnecessarily.

Pearl: K replete empirically despite 'normal' levels (total body K profoundly depleted). DKA fluid resus 0.9 % NS → 0.45 % NS once corrected Na normal → add D5 when glucose < 200.

Pitfall: bicarbonate — only if pH < 6.9 (ADA). Routine bicarb worsens hypoK, paradoxical CSF acidosis.
ref: ADA DKA Guidelines

stem: Thyroid storm management (Burch-Wartofsky ≥ 45). Best regimen?
options: Beta-blocker + thionamide + iodine (given 1 h after thionamide) + hydrocortisone
explanation:
Why combo + sequencing: propranolol 1-2 mg IV q 15 min (blocks T4→T3 conversion peripherally + rate control); propylthiouracil 200 mg q 4 h OR methimazole 20 mg q 4 h (blocks synthesis); iodine (Lugol's 8 drops q 6 h OR K iodide) 1 HOUR AFTER thionamide (Wolff-Chaikoff — iodine would otherwise fuel storage); hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q 8 h (blocks peripheral conversion + treats possible adrenal insufficiency).

Why not others: iodine FIRST → stuffs thyroid with substrate = disaster; thionamide alone slow; steroids alone insufficient.

Pearl: treat precipitant (infection, non-adherence, iodine contrast, surgery). Cholestyramine binds thyroid hormones in gut. PLEX for refractory cases.

Pitfall: β-blockers caution in severe HF (storm can cause high-output failure that converts to decompensated).
ref: Chiha M et al. Thyroid storm. J Intensive Care Med 2015

stem: Adrenal crisis presentation + treatment?
options: Shock + hypoNa + hyperK + hypoglycaemia; give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV STAT + saline + glucose
explanation:
Why hydrocort stat: adrenal crisis = life-threatening. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus → 50 mg q 6 h (or infusion 200 mg/24 h). IV NS for shock. D50 for hypoglycaemia. Treat precipitant.

Why not others: HTN is wrong — Addisonian crisis has HYPOtension; oral inadequate; thyroid replacement before cortisol in combined pan-hypopit → adrenal crisis.

Pearl: precipitants — sepsis, surgery, steroid withdrawal. If uncertain, give cortisol and send random cortisol / ACTH before (results won't delay).

Pitfall: dexamethasone 4 mg IV does NOT interfere with cortisol assay and can be given empirically pending cortisol levels (then switch to hydrocortisone).
ref: Bornstein SR et al. Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines. JCEM 2016

stem: Variceal haemorrhage in cirrhosis — immediate management includes all EXCEPT?
explanation:
Why not high-dose albumin: 100 mL/kg is absurd. Albumin is used for large-volume paracentesis (6-8 g per L removed) or SBP (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3), not variceal bleed resus.

Why the others are correct: octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow; ceftriaxone 1 g IV reduces mortality in cirrhotic GIB (SBP prophylaxis); endoscopy < 12 h for band ligation.

Pearl: TIPS for refractory bleed. Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore) is a bridge (only hours — mucosal necrosis).

Pitfall: transfuse restrictively (Hb < 7) in variceal bleed — Villanueva NEJM 2013 showed liberal transfusion worsens rebleeding + mortality.
ref: de Franchis R. Baveno VII Consensus. J Hepatol 2022

stem: Severe acute pancreatitis — initial resuscitation volume?
explanation:
Why moderate resus: WATERFALL trial (NEJM 2022) — aggressive fluids (20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/hr) caused MORE fluid overload than moderate (10 mL/kg bolus then 1.5 mL/kg/hr) without outcome benefit. Current guidance: moderate titrated resus with Ringer's lactate.

Why not others: 200 mL/kg over-resus; strict NPO delays nutrition (early EN within 48 h now preferred); colloid no benefit.

Pearl: early (24-48 h) oral/enteral feeding reduces infection + mortality (PYTHON trial). Antibiotics NOT prophylactic — only for proven infected necrosis.

Pitfall: aggressive fluids in elderly cardiac patient → ARDS, abdominal compartment syndrome.
ref: de-Madaria E et al. WATERFALL. NEJM 2022;387:989-1000

stem: Toxic megacolon indications for surgery?
options: Peritonitis, perforation, severe haemorrhage, or failure of medical therapy in 24-72 h
explanation:
Why these indications: emergency colectomy for peritonitis, perforation, massive bleeding, or failure to improve in 24-72 h of maximal medical therapy (IV steroids, bowel rest, cyclosporine or infliximab rescue).

Why not others: immediate surgery for all is excessive; 2 weeks too late; never surgical is wrong.

Pearl: avoid anticholinergics, opioids, loperamide — can precipitate megacolon. Daily plain X-ray to monitor colonic diameter (> 6 cm = toxic).

Pitfall: steroid taper too fast → relapse. Cyclosporine or infliximab IV as rescue therapy (not both together — infection risk).
ref: Autenrieth DM, Baumgart DC. Toxic megacolon. Inflamm Bowel Dis 2012

stem: Optimal timing to start enteral nutrition in ICU patient without contraindication?
explanation:
Why 24-48 h: ASPEN/SCCM — early EN < 24-48 h in critically ill improves mortality, reduces infection, preserves gut integrity. Trophic feeds (10-20 mL/hr) are acceptable in ARDS (EDEN trial).

Why not others: delay → gut atrophy + bacterial translocation; 'hungry' ignores physiology.

Pearl: PN only if EN contraindicated (bowel obstruction, severe shock on vasopressors, active GI bleed). Delay PN to day 7 in well-nourished (EPaNIC 2011).

Pitfall: head-of-bed 30° to reduce VAP. Residual volume checks lack evidence to guide intolerance — abandon.
ref: McClave SA et al. ASPEN/SCCM Nutrition Guidelines. JPEN 2016

stem: Refeeding syndrome risk factors include all EXCEPT?
explanation:
Why NOT BMI > 30: refeeding syndrome occurs in MALNOURISHED patients when feeds restart. Low BMI, significant weight loss, prolonged starvation, alcoholism, cancer, anorexia nervosa are high risk.

Why others ARE risk factors: BMI < 16 (major); > 10 d minimal intake; alcoholism (B1 deficiency + poor nutrition).

Pearl: prevention — thiamine 100-300 mg IV before food; start feeds at 5-10 kcal/kg/day, advance over 4-7 days; replete K, Mg, PO₄ aggressively with labs q 12 h × 72 h.

Pitfall: glucose infusion (D5 at TKO) alone in malnourished can precipitate Wernicke — always thiamine FIRST.
ref: NICE CG32. Nutrition Support. 2006 (updated 2017)

stem: Protein target in septic ICU patient on CRRT?
explanation:
Why 1.5-2 g/kg: critical illness drives catabolism. CRRT losses add to deficit (amino acids pass through filter). ASPEN/SCCM — 1.2-2.0 g/kg (actual BW in non-obese, ideal BW in obese); 1.5-2.0 specifically in burns, severe sepsis, CRRT.

Why not others: 0.8 is healthy-adult need; 1.2 is lower end for ICU; 3 g/kg excessive (no outcome benefit, azotaemia risk).

Pearl: no mortality signal from higher-vs-lower protein (NUTRIREA-2, EFFORT Protein trials). Individualise. Monitor UUN for adequacy if feasible.

Pitfall: protein targets not met in most ICU patients — feeding interruptions (procedures, intolerance) → 50-70 % of target actually delivered.
ref: McClave SA et al. ASPEN/SCCM Nutrition Guidelines. JPEN 2016

stem: SBT (spontaneous breathing trial) failure in a patient on pressure support — best next step?
options: Return to full ventilator support, identify cause of failure, reassess next day
explanation:
Why return + assess: failed SBT → rest overnight, don't push. Identify cause — cardiac (high PCWP, failing LV), respiratory (airway resistance, muscle weakness), volume overload, delirium, pain.

Why not others: reintubate if not already intubated? assumes extubation; longer SBT doesn't address root cause; diuretic without cause is random.

Pearl: RSBI (RR/TV in L) < 105 at end of SBT predicts success; > 105 predicts failure. SAT (spontaneous awakening trial — stop sedation) paired with SBT (ABC trial) accelerates liberation.

Pitfall: cuff-leak test before extubation if high-risk airway (long intubation, trauma, repeat intubation) — < 110 mL leak → dexamethasone 20 mg × 24 h pre-extubation.
ref: Yang KL, Tobin MJ. RSBI. NEJM 1991 · Girard TD et al. ABC. Lancet 2008

stem: Post-extubation for COPD / cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — best support to reduce reintubation?
explanation:
Why NIV in these groups: COPD and cardiogenic oedema — NIV reduces reintubation + mortality post-extubation (Nava 2005). In hypoxic respiratory failure without hypercapnia, HFNC may be first-line (FLORALI).

Why not others: nasal cannula insufficient; HFNC equivalent/inferior to NIV in COPD/cardiogenic; routine reintubation un-necessary.

Pearl: prophylactic NIV in high-risk extubation (age > 65, CHF, APACHE > 12) reduces reintubation.

Pitfall: NIV failure signs — persistent tachypnoea > 30, PaCO₂ not improving, worsening pH, agitation / mental status decline. Reintubate early; don't delay.
ref: Thille AW et al. HFNC vs NIV post-extubation. JAMA 2019;322:1465-75

stem: CAM-ICU positive requires?
options: Feature 1 (acute change/fluctuating) + 2 (inattention) + either 3 (altered LOC) OR 4 (disorganised thinking)
explanation:
Why F1 + F2 + (F3 OR F4): validated CAM-ICU algorithm — acute change in mental status OR fluctuating + inattention (ASE Letters — > 2 errors) + either altered LOC (RASS ≠ 0) OR disorganised thinking.

Why not others: all 4 is wrong (over-specific); features 3/4 alone miss acuity; any 1 insufficient.

Pearl: always assess RASS first — a RASS of − 4/− 5 is 'unarousable', not assessable for delirium. Daily screening every shift.

Pitfall: 'inattentive' sedated patient may actually have hyperactive delirium under sedation — lift sedation, reassess.
ref: Ely EW et al. CAM-ICU. JAMA 2001

stem: Preferred sedation in ICU to reduce delirium?
explanation:
Why non-benzos: PADIS 2018 + SPICE-III — avoid benzodiazepine infusions when possible (strong association with delirium). Propofol or dexmedetomidine preferred. Dexmedetomidine does not depress respiration + preserves arousable sleep architecture.

Why not others: midazolam/lorazepam infusions ↑ delirium; deep sedation → longer ICU, more delirium, PTSD — target LIGHT sedation (RASS 0 to − 2).

Pearl: ABCDEF bundle — Assess pain, Both SAT+SBT, Choice of sedation (light, non-benzo), Delirium assess+treat, Early mobility, Family engagement — reduces ICU mortality.

Pitfall: haloperidol / quetiapine have no mortality benefit for delirium (MIND-USA). Use for safety (severe agitation) only — not as a 'cure'.
ref: Devlin JW et al. PADIS 2018 · Girard TD et al. MIND-USA. NEJM 2018
